title: A Lament for the Proud Ship Tyre
summary: Ezekiel sings a funeral song for Tyre, pictured as a magnificent merchant ship built from the finest materials of the known world and crewed by the best sailors. A long catalog lists the nations that traded with her and the goods they exchanged. Then the east wind shatters the ship in the heart of the sea, and all who lived by her trade stand on the shore and mourn.
story: Chapter 26 announced Tyre's fall in the language of siege and conquest. Chapter 27 retells the same fall as a shipwreck and a funeral. Its long list of trading partners makes the reader feel the sheer reach of Tyre's commercial empire, which makes the sudden sinking all the more shocking. The chapter continues the book's section against the nations (chapters 25 to 32) and prepares for chapter 28, where the king of Tyre is addressed directly. Tyre's claim in verse 3, I am perfect in beauty, is the pride the next chapter will expose at its root.
historical:
The chapter is one of the most detailed descriptions of ancient international trade to survive from the Iron Age, and it names places from Spain to Mesopotamia and from Anatolia to Arabia. Senir is another name for Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9); Bashan, east of the Jordan, was famed for its oaks; Lebanon for its cedars. Sidon, Arvad, and Gebal (the city the Greeks called Byblos) were other Phoenician cities. Tarshish was a distant western port, often identified with Tartessus in southern Spain, though other locations have been proposed. Javan refers to the Ionian Greeks, while Tubal and Meshech were peoples of Anatolia, in modern Turkey. Dedan, Sheba, Raamah, and Kedar were trading peoples and tribes of Arabia; Haran and Asshur lay in upper Mesopotamia. A few names, such as Helech, Gammad, and Chilmad, are uncertain.

The list reflects Tyre at the height of its commercial power in the seventh and early sixth centuries BC, when Phoenician ships dominated much of the Mediterranean and its merchants linked sea trade to the overland caravan routes of Arabia and Mesopotamia. Judah and Israel appear in verse 17 as suppliers of wheat, honey, oil, and balm, a reminder that Tyre's wealth and Jerusalem's economy had long been intertwined.
cultural:
Phoenician ships were famous across the ancient world, and the details of Ezekiel's ship are realistic: planking, mast, oars, a deck inlaid with ivory, an embroidered linen sail, and an awning dyed blue and purple. Purple dye, extracted in tiny quantities from murex sea snails, was Tyre's most famous product and was so costly that it became the color of royalty. The goods in the catalog run from metals (silver, iron, tin, lead) to horses, ivory and ebony, textiles, grain, wine, spices, gold, and precious stones. Slaves appear too (verse 13), a sober reminder that human beings were traded alongside bronze vessels.

The mourning of verses 29 to 32 follows known customs: throwing dust on the head, rolling in ashes, shaving the head, and putting on sackcloth, the coarse cloth worn in grief. The hissing of verse 36 was a sound of shock and horror at a ruin, not necessarily of contempt.
literary: The chapter is a qinah, a funeral lament, and much of it is poetry in the lament's limping rhythm. It is built as an extended metaphor with a prose catalog set in the middle. Verses 3 to 11 describe the ship's construction and crew; verses 12 to 25 list Tyre's trading partners and their goods, possibly drawing on a real trade list, in a repeated formula (they exchanged ... for your wares); verses 26 to 36 return to poetry and describe the wreck and the mourning. The contrast is deliberate. The long, leisurely list of wealth builds up the ship's cargo line by line, and then a single east wind sinks it all. Beauty is a key word: Tyre claims to be perfect in beauty (verse 3), and the builders and soldiers perfected her beauty (verses 4 and 11).

outline.t: A lament for Tyre, who says, I am perfect in beauty
The splendid ship: materials and crew
The catalog of trading partners and goods
The east wind shatters the ship
The lament: who was ever like Tyre?

doctrines.note: Tyre's fault is pride in its own beauty and wealth (verse 3). The chapter shows how prosperity can become a kind of self-worship, and how a whole economy can be built on it.
One east wind is enough to sink everything Tyre built. The chapter pictures God's judgment as the sudden end of a security that seemed permanent.
The catalog is also a picture of the created world's richness: timber, metals, animals, grain, spices, and craft. The goods are not condemned; the pride that treated them as the measure of worth is.

words.note: Rakhal, to trade or go about as a merchant. Its forms appear ten times in the chapter, and the repetition makes trade the city's very identity. Tyre is called merchant of the peoples (verse 3).

Yophi, beauty. Tyre's boast is that it is perfect in beauty, and the chapter shows the beauty as real: fine wood, linen, purple, ivory. The problem is not the beauty but the claim of perfection, which the next chapter applies to Tyre's king.

Argaman, purple, the red-purple dye for which Phoenicia was famous. It also colored the tabernacle curtains and priestly garments (Exodus 26:1; 28:5-6), so an Israelite reader would recognize it as the color of splendor and holiness.

Mallach, a sailor or mariner, a word often linked to the Hebrew for salt, though it may be a loanword from Akkadian. The sailors who once made Tyre great are the ones who stand on the shore to mourn her (verse 29).

christ: Revelation 18 draws directly on this chapter in its lament over the fall of Babylon the great. There too merchants and sea captains stand far off, throw dust on their heads, and weep over a city whose trade made them rich, and a long list of cargoes is recited, ending with slaves, that is, human souls (Revelation 18:11-19). John uses Ezekiel's Tyre as a picture of every proud, wealthy world order that trades in everything, including people. Against it the New Testament sets the city of God, whose glory is God's presence rather than its commerce (Revelation 21:22-26), and Jesus' warning that a person's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions (Luke 12:15). The link here is a thematic one drawn by later writers, who saw in Tyre a pattern that repeats.
questions: Tyre's list of trading partners is impressive, and the whole thing sank in a moment. What do you rely on that might look permanent but is not?
Slaves appear in the catalog of goods (verse 13). Where does modern trade still treat people as merchandise, and what does that ask of us?
Tyre said, I am perfect in beauty. How can we enjoy real beauty and skill without turning them into pride?
